english.html: And this kind of fault, although at the execution there was some will, caused by this or a like passion, nevertheless, because such will was not premeditated nor deliberate, but rather forced and constrained by passion <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, is easily pardoned <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>, especially since it is very difficult for a man so justly provoked to restrain and master himself <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup> — witness him who dared to lay hand upon Pope John XIII and cut his throat, having found him misconducting himself with his wife <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>. Crimes not voluntarily committed are those which are excused as fortuitous, and by some disaster of error or ignorance <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>: as when Telegonus, son of Ulysses and of Circe, by chance killed his father, not knowing him, and thinking he had to do with the servants, who would not allow him entry into his father's house <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>. As likewise if, at the hunt, thinking to hurl the dart against a roe-deer, a boar, or other wild beast, one should meet with a man who died or was wounded by that blow <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. And in the deed which here presents itself: if a woman, thinking she has to do with her husband, is known by another, or a man, believing he approaches his wife, converses with another, both are more worthy of excuse than of penalty <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>, as we shall discourse more amply hereafter. Otherwise Lot would have been incestuous when he got his two daughters with child, believing he had to do with his wife <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>. Certainly such kinds of offences, inasmuch as they proceed from no evil will, seem to be excusable <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>; unless there were some preceding evil work which had occasioned this deed <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>: for already he who committed the crime was in fault, exercising an act in itself evil and reprobate, whence his intention, considering the beginning, was corrupted and depraved. As for example: if I have the will to murder Antoine, and, thinking to slay him, I kill François, I am not excused: for my purpose has always been to kill a man <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 4.2 (Quod metus causa gestum erit), l. Si mulier (cf. D. 4.2.21, Paul), the penultimate paragraph (unverified)
notes.original: l. ſi mulier P. penult. D. quod met. ca.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2 (De furtis), l. Verum (fragment not identified); and D. 1.1.3, l. Ut vim, cited at {i}
notes.original: l. verum. D. de fur. l. vt vĩ alleguee.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5.39 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis, l. Si adulterium cum incesto, Papinian; 48.5.38 in some editions), § Imperator (§ 8)
notes.original: l. ſi adulte rium. P. imp. D. de adult.
notes.gloss: The rescript of Marcus and Commodus: the husband who kills his wife taken in adultery, impetu tractus doloris, "carried away by the impulse of grief", does not suffer the full penalty of the lex Cornelia de sicariis, because it is most difficult to restrain a just grief (difficillimum est iustum dolorem temperare).

notes.citation: Platina (Bartolomeo Sacchi), Lives of the Popes (Liber de vita Christi ac omnium pontificum), the life of John XIII in Platina's count
notes.original: Platina en la vie des pa-pes.
notes.gloss: Platina's John XIII is the modern John XII (Octavian), said to have been struck down by the husband of a woman with whom he was taken in adultery, and to have died within days; Coras's luy couper la gorge sharpens the story.

notes.citation: Digest 48.19.11.2, l. Respiciendum (Perspiciendum), the penultimate paragraph as printed (the law has only §§ 1–2 in the modern division; the chance-killing is in § 2, cited at {c}); and D. 1.3.1–2, cited at {b}
notes.original: l. reſpicien dum P. penul. D. de pœn. l. j. & ij. D. de legib.
notes.gloss: Casu vero, cum in venando telum in feram missum hominem interfecit — "by chance, as when in hunting a weapon aimed at a beast kills a man".

notes.citation: Ovid, Fasti, book III as cited (3.92 names Telegonus as founder of Tusculum; the killing of Ulysses by his son Telegonus is told in the epic Telegony, in Hyginus, Fabulae 127, and alluded to in Ovid, Ibis 567–568 — the detail that Telegonus took his father for a servant is not in these)
Decretals X 5.12 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. Lator (chapter number unverified); and D. 48.19.11.2, the last paragraph of l. Respiciendum, cited at {c}
notes.original: c. lator. de homicid. P. final de la l. reſpiciẽdum. alleguee.

notes.citation: Gratian, Decretum, C. 31 q. 1 c. 1 as printed (unverified); and the chapters Si virgo and In lectum at "C. 33 q. 2" as printed — these two chapters, on the woman who lies with a man she takes for her husband, stand in the modern division at C. 34 qq. 1–2 (chapter numbers unverified)
notes.original: c. j xxxi q. j c. ſi virgo C. in lectũ. xxxiij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: The chapter Si virgo is cited again at annot-077 {a} for the rule that such a woman is not an adulteress until she knows.

notes.citation: Genesis 19 (19:30–38, Lot and his daughters); and Gratian, Decretum, C. 15 q. 1, c. Inebriaverunt (chapter number unverified)
notes.original: Geneſe c. xix. c. inebria uerũt xv q j.
notes.gloss: C. 15 q. 1 treats offences committed in drunkenness or madness; the chapter takes its incipit from Lot's daughters making their father drunk.

notes.citation: Digest 9.2.11 (Ad legem Aquiliam, l. Item Mela, Ulpian); and Decretals X 5.12, c. Lator, cited at {q}
notes.original: l item Mel la. D. ad l. Aquil. c. lator allegué.
notes.gloss: Item Mela scribit, si, cum pila quidam luderent… — the ball that strikes the barber's hand so that he cuts the slave's throat: the classic case of liability without evil intent, where fault lies with whoever acted carelessly.

notes.citation: Digest 48.8.1 (Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis et veneficis, l. Lege Cornelia, Marcian), § 1; Digest 9.2 (Ad legem Aquiliam), l. Qui servus (?) at the paragraph Si fornicarius — not identified; and Decretals X 5.12, c. Continebatur (chapter number unverified)
notes.original: l. lege. P. j de ſiccar. l. q ſeruus. D. ſi fornicarius. D. ad l. Aqui. c. contine latur. de homi.
notes.gloss: The transcription's contine latur is Continebatur; l. q ſeruus is probably l. qui servus or l. quod servus, but no fragment of D. 9.2 with a paragraph Si fornicarius could be identified.

notes.citation: Digest 9.2.45 (Ad legem Aquiliam, l. Scientiam, Paul), § 4, the last paragraph; Digest 47.10 (De iniuriis et famosis libellis), l. Cum qui (?), § Si iniuria — fragment not identified (cf. D. 47.10.4, Paul: he who, meaning to strike his slave, unwillingly strikes a bystander, is not liable for iniuria); and Bartolus (Bartole) on D. 48.19.11, l. Respiciendum, at the last paragraph
notes.original: l ſcientiam. P. final. D. ad l. Aquil. l. cũ qui. P. ſi iniu ria. D. de iniu riis. Bartole en la l. reſpiciendum. P. final.
notes.gloss: D. 9.2.45.4: si defendendi mei causa lapidem in adversarium misero, sed non eum, sed praetereuntem percussero, tenebor lege Aquilia — if, defending myself, I throw a stone at my adversary and hit a passer-by instead, I am liable: the stone meant for one man and striking another, which is Coras's Antoine and François.
